finding.claim: The avatar endpoint fetches a user-supplied URL server-side. The only check is that the string starts with "https://". There is no host or IP allowlist, no block on private, loopback or link-local addresses, and no DNS-resolution check. Axios follows redirects by default, so an attacker-controlled HTTPS server can redirect to internal targets, including plain http:// ones, and the scheme check does not apply to redirect hops. An attacker can reach internal HTTPS services, cloud metadata endpoints that serve HTTPS, and hosts such as https://localhost:PORT or https://10.x.x.x. They can also probe internal ports and hosts, because the response reveals the byte length and error behaviour.

trace.note: url = req.body.avatarUrl, read directly from the request body
only validation: typeof string and startsWith("https://"); no host, IP or redirect restrictions
axios.get(url) issues the outbound request with default redirect following (maxRedirects 5)
response size is returned to the caller, which gives a blind or semi-blind oracle for internal resources

finding.guards_checked: The https:// prefix check is the only guard. It does not restrict the host. It does not prevent redirects to http:// or internal hosts. It does not stop DNS rebinding or hostnames that resolve to private IPs. No authentication middleware is present. No allowlist, no maxRedirects setting and no custom agent or lookup hook was found.

verdict.guard_found: none (only a typeof string and startsWith("https://") scheme-prefix check at server.js:11)
verdict.reason: server.js:10 takes req.body.avatarUrl unauthenticated, server.js:11 only checks the "https://" prefix (not a closing guard), and server.js:14 passes it to axios.get with default redirects, with the byte length returned at server.js:15.
